description: We are three nuns and a penguin and we are very excited about participating in this year's NASA space apps Hackathon.
summary: Analyzing potential water sources on Mars is the first step in the mission of sending humans to explore our "Red Planet" for the first time. Notably, a substantial source of hydrogen will allow astronauts to create fuel for the way back to Earth. The goal of our project is to facilitate sample collection of potential water sources on Mars (glaciers, aqueous minerals, hydrous minerals) through the identification of three things: sites that have optimal conditions for a human-carrying spacecraft to land safely, sites whose soil is very likely to contain ice and/or minerals indicative of past or present traces of water, and the optimal path between the two sites considering topological and atmospheric conditions.
details:
The main goal of our project lies in the identification of 3 things:

  1. Sites that have optimal conditions for a human-carrying spacecraft to land safely
  2. Sites whose soil is very likely to contain ice and/or minerals indicative of past traces of water
  3. The optimal path between the two sites considering topological and atmospheric conditions

When the user opens the project, they will be able to click anywhere on the heatmap to select their landing site. We’ve determined this heatmap by layering several maps which detail different conditions and by analyzing this layering to determine the optimal zones (in green). We selected the layers by basing ourselves off of the conditions for a successful landing:

  • Elevation (thus, atmosphere density)
  • Dust
  • Thermal inertia

Regions in green are thus regions where all these 4 criteria are optimized. We used QGIS to layer and analyze the data.

Then, the region that the user clicked on is zoomed in to reveal the possible collecting sites nearby, and an optimal path is traced to it. 

Collection sites were identified using data points of glaciers, aqueous minerals, and hydrous minerals, as the presence of these elements in a given area is indicative of a past (or present!) water presence. Sampling martian rock containing these substances allows researchers to better understand the historical and the future habitability of the planet. 

The optimal path between your landing site and a certain collection site is then identified using a dijkstra algorithm.

Essentially, the topographic map surrounding your landing site is turned into a black and white grid, where white signifies a place where you can walk and black is somewhere you cannot walk. A black versus white pixel is chosen based on the degree to which the topography is changing in that location. 

So based on the white available pixels, the algorithm will find the fastest path to the collection site, which is displayed on the front end. 

Now there are a lot of available data collection sites, but we only want the sites that are less than 100km away, so already we can eliminate most of them. With the few that remain, we use the dijkstra algorithm to find the fastest path for each and then we choose the data collection site with the fastest path among them.
